data.title: Hyperscaler Stocks Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet Report Next Week – Here’s What Dan Ives Expects
data.description:
The earnings season volume gets pumped up next week, when three of the biggest spenders on AI infrastructure release their latest quarterly results. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) will report on Wednesday, with Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) following on Thursday.

The reports land at a nervous moment for the market. Meta’s spending headlines, a 10-year Treasury yield hovering around 5%, higher oil prices and ongoing talk of an AI bubble have all weighed on sentiment.

However, tech bull analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives thinks the results should ease that anxiety rather than deepen it. He frames his view with two figures. Hyperscalers will spend about $850 billion on AI this year, while their cloud backlog tops $2 trillion and is growing faster than sales. To Ives, that gap means these companies are short of capacity, not customers. He expects another round of higher spending forecasts, and he argues the money is going toward signed contracts rather than speculative buildouts.

Promotion

Want cash flow from the tech industry without leaving it? Meet TDAQ.

Ives has laid out expectations for each of these tech giants ahead of the anticipated prints, so let’s see what he’s looking for.

Microsoft

Microsoft is on Ives’ list of five favorite tech names heading into 2027, and he sees it as the “cleanest expression of that setup.” For fiscal Q1 2027, analysts expect revenue of $90.6 billion, a 17% year-over-year gain, and adjusted EPS of $4.73. Azure is projected near the upper end of management’s 44% to 45% constant-currency outlook. Azure usually drives the share price, but Ives is more focused on whether new capacity gets filled as fast as it arrives. In his view, a backlog that grows faster than revenue is what supports the heavy investment.

He also wants Copilot seat counts and Foundry to show that AI agents are becoming a source of revenue in their own right. Spending will rise again, but the analyst points out that Microsoft can cover it with cash from its existing businesses and still grow operating income by double digits.

Ives reiterated his Outperform (i.e., Buy) rating and $615 price target, suggesting the stock will gain 17% over the coming months.

On the Street, MSFT holds a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 34 Buys and 2 Holds, and the average price target of $607.62 implies 16% upside from current levels. (See MSFT stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Mind the Gap,’ Says Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
For decades, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) was one of tech’s most dependable cash generators. It sold database software to large companies that rarely switched vendors. Growth was modest, but the money kept coming in. Then the company changed course and went all in on AI, agreeing to build and power huge amounts of data center capacity, with OpenAI as its biggest customer.

The move has split shareholders. Some see Oracle becoming a major cloud player. Others see a balance sheet under real pressure. Against that backdrop, the stock has struggled this year, shedding 35%, and S&P Global’s July decision to cut Oracle’s credit rating to BBB-, the lowest investment-grade tier, made things worse.

An investor using the moniker Trapping Value (TV) has been watching the credit side of the story and thinks equity investors are underestimating it.

Promotion

Explore ORCZ for 2X short leverage on ORCL

The first issue is the scale of spending. Oracle has guided to $90 billion–$95 billion in capital expenditures for fiscal 2027, which ends in May, and estimates for the following year are close to $100 billion. In fiscal 2024, the company spent under $7 billion, so spending is on track to rise about 14-fold in four years. Much of that money goes toward OpenAI contracts, including a $300 billion, five-year deal that begins in 2027. TV points out that OpenAI is itself losing large sums of money, which makes Oracle’s huge contract backlog less reassuring than the headline figure suggests.

TV sees a sizable gap in the cash math. Operating cash flow won’t come close to covering capex, and dividends and maturing debt also have to be paid. S&P expects a free operating cash flow deficit of nearly $42 billion in fiscal 2027, narrowing to about $25 billion in fiscal 2028. Total debt is already approaching $160 billion.

TV also looks to the bond market for clues. Oracle’s longer-dated bonds yield around 8.8%, according to the investor, roughly 2.8 percentage points more than a benchmark index of long-term investment-grade corporate bonds. In TV’s view, bond investors are pricing in more risk than the official rating suggests.

If borrowing becomes too expensive, the remaining option is issuing stock. Oracle has already sold $5 billion in mandatory convertible preferred shares and plans another $20 billion in equity. TV thinks more dilution could follow if the company keeps spending near $100 billion a year, which would cut into per-share earnings even if OpenAI meets all its commitments.

On the plus side, TV acknowledges that Oracle’s core software business remains solid and that S&P expects the cash shortfall to narrow as profits improve. Still, with funding costs rising and dilution likely, TV prefers to stay on the sidelines for now and rates ORCL a Hold (i.e., Neutral). (To watch Trapping Value’s track record, click here)

Overall, the Street is far more upbeat. Based on a mix of 27 Buys, 4 Holds and 1 Sell, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. At $244.89, the average price target points to 12-month returns of 95%. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: SK hynix vs. Micron: Which Memory Stock Has the Edge for the Long Haul? Top Investor Weighs In
data.description:
Memory chips have long been one of the most cyclical corners of the semiconductor world. When demand is strong, prices jump and manufacturers race to add capacity, until the new capacity floods the market and prices crash. The AI boom has interrupted that pattern, at least for now. Only three companies make memory at real scale: SK hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY), Micron (NASDAQ:MU), and Samsung. Samsung is the odd one out, since its memory business sits alongside phones, TVs, and other products. Together the three control more than 85% of the DRAM market and over 60% of NAND flash, so when data center builders all need huge amounts of memory at once, these companies set the terms.

American investors can now compare SK hynix and Micron more directly. South Korea’s SK hynix began trading on the Nasdaq through American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) in July. Top investor Geoffrey Seiler, a contributor to The Motley Fool, has looked at both to see which one deserves a place in a portfolio.

The 5-star investor starts with high bandwidth memory, or HBM. This specialized DRAM sits right next to GPUs and other AI accelerators so data reaches them fast enough to keep those costly chips busy. The more computing power the industry needs, the more HBM it needs too, and all three memory makers have shifted their attention toward it. Adding supply is slow, though. Seiler explains that key HBM components require extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, which only ASML builds. Makers of GPUs and other logic chips need those same machines, so there aren’t enough to go around. Each HBM chip also uses roughly triple the wafer space of a standard DRAM chip.

Promotion

Curious why XOVR invested in Kalshi? Explore the long-term strategy behind the investment.

Since manufacturers have shifted so much capacity to HBM, ordinary DRAM and NAND are now in short supply as well. NAND is getting an extra boost from AI companies buying enormous SSDs to hold their training data. The upshot is that prices for everyday memory have climbed faster than HBM prices. Seiler, who ranks among the top 4% of investors on TipRanks, says this is worth keeping in mind when weighing the two companies against each other.

SK hynix leads in HBM. In the second quarter, it held half of that market, along with 25% of DRAM and 19% of NAND. Nvidia buys more HBM from SK hynix than from anyone else, and in July the two sides signed a long-term partnership valued at more than $500 billion that covers memory supply and AI data center buildouts. Micron had a similar DRAM share of 24%, but only 18% of HBM. It ranks third in NAND with a 15% share. Micron has signed 26 long-term agreements that cover more than 35% of its revenue through 2030.

Both companies get about 73% of their sales from DRAM. Seiler notes that while both are shipping more chips, pricing accounts for most of the gains. Because commodity memory has outpaced HBM, Micron has grown faster. Its fiscal fourth-quarter revenue rose 379% year over year, and gross margin roughly doubled to 86.8%. SK hynix’s revenue grew 257%, and its gross margin rose from 54% to 83%.

So, which one offers a better opportunity right now?

Both stocks trade at single-digit multiples of forward earnings, or “bargain-basement valuations,” as Seiler puts it, which suggests investors expect the boom to fade. Seiler sees that as the key risk. HBM makes up only a small part of Micron’s sales, so the company would take a bigger hit if prices for standard memory fall back, even with its long-term contracts in place. “As such, I think that, as the HBM and advanced memory technology leader with strong ties to Nvidia, SK hynix is ultimately the better memory stock to own over the long term,” Seiler summed up. (To watch Seiler’s track record, click here)

On Wall Street, both stocks are seen as safe bets, with the pair claiming Strong Buy consensus ratings. Both are also expected to generate big returns over the next year. SKHY’s average price target lands at $254.70, suggesting the stock will gain 88%. MU is expected to climb 88% higher, given the average target clocks in at $1,621.67. data.title: RKLB vs. ASTS: One Space Stock Is a Buying Opportunity, the Other Is One to Avoid, Says Investor
data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) and AST SpaceMobile (NASDAQ:ASTS) are two names operating in the space sector that have been getting plenty of attention over the past year. Rocket Lab builds satellites and flies its own launch vehicles. AST SpaceMobile is trying to put a network of large satellites into orbit that connect directly to ordinary smartphones through mobile carrier partners.

After surging dramatically earlier in the year, both stocks have had a rough few months. Rocket Lab is down about 66% from its peak, and AST SpaceMobile has fallen roughly 71% from its own high. Much of the sector’s momentum faded once SpaceX went public and drew investor attention toward itself. Despite the shared slump, the two companies stand on very different footing.

That difference is what an investor using the pseudonym The Alpha Analyst (AA) focuses on, considering which of the two offers a sounder way to stay invested in the space theme.

Promotion

High conviction ASTS bulls now have this Tradr ETF

For AA, the core issue is how much each company controls its own destiny. Rocket Lab does almost everything in-house. It flies the small Electron rocket and a suborbital version called HASTE, and it is developing Neutron, a larger reusable vehicle. Satellite building is actually its biggest earner, bringing in roughly $189.5 million of about $234 million in Q2 sales. So even though Neutron has yet to make its first flight, the rest of the business keeps moving.

AST SpaceMobile is in a much tighter spot. It needs other companies to launch its BlueBird satellites, chiefly SpaceX and Blue Origin, and a Blue Origin mission left BlueBird 7 stuck in a useless orbit in April. The SpaceX reliance is especially uncomfortable. SpaceX recently won FCC approval for 15,000 next-generation mobile satellites and bought low-band spectrum, aiming to become a major US carrier through Starlink Mobile. That would put it in direct competition with the telecom firms AST depends on.

AA had previously held back on Rocket Lab because its path to profitability depended on Neutron. Management linked its first positive adjusted EBITDA quarter to the period after Neutron’s debut. The planned purchase of Iridium changes that. Iridium runs a satellite phone and data network with 66 satellites and around 2.5 million subscribers. It generated about $872 million in revenue and roughly $495 million in operating EBITDA in 2025, while Rocket Lab is guiding to a Q3 loss of about $17-23 million.

Once the deal closes, likely around mid-2027, the combined company should be EBITDA positive with or without Neutron. Iridium also serves a niche market rather than taking on SpaceX directly. Meanwhile, Rocket Lab’s backlog has grown to about $2.36 billion, and close to half of it is expected to become revenue within a year.

AST’s picture looks very different. It has only about 13 of the roughly 45 satellites it needs for continuous coverage in key markets, and that target has now slid into early 2027. Its $1 billion revenue ambition was once tied to 2027 but is now described only as the first full year of commercial service. Analysts also keep trimming their FY2027 forecasts. For AA, the difference is that AST has no other business to fall back on while it waits for launches, so a sharp drop in the share price isn’t enough reason to turn positive while forecasts are still heading down.

Valuation is where things get less clear-cut. On FY2028 numbers, AST trades at roughly 8x EV/Sales, while Rocket Lab sits near 16.4x for broadly similar revenue, and that Rocket Lab figure doesn’t yet include Iridium. AA thinks the premium is justified by the quality and reliability of Rocket Lab’s revenue.

Meanwhile, the upcoming Q3 results will be the first real test. For Rocket Lab, weak margins are already expected, so bookings, backlog and Neutron progress matter more. AST faces a tougher test. It booked only about $46 million in first-half revenue against a $150-200 million full-year target, so the second half needs a big step up, and a soft quarter could force a guidance cut. On Rocket Lab’s side, AA flags regulatory delays to the Iridium deal and further Neutron setbacks as the main risks.

Weighing it all up, The Alpha Analyst has now upgraded Rocket Lab from Hold (i.e., Neutral) to Buy and keeps a Sell rating on AST SpaceMobile. (To watch The Alpha Analyst’s track record, click here)

The Street only partially agrees, giving RKLB a Strong Buy consensus view, while ASTS is rated a Moderate Buy. The former is expected to gain 92% over the next year, given its average price target lands at $98.25. ASTS’s average target stands at $80.10, a figure pointing to even more robust upside of 107%. (See RKLB stock forecast or ASTS stock forecast)

data.title: Meta vs. Netflix: Oppenheimer Says Only One Stock Is a Buy After Rocky Earnings
data.description:
It’s turning out to be a bit of a rough week for two of the internet’s biggest names. Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) both beat Wall Street’s profit estimates for the third quarter, and investors sold both stocks anyway. Meta’s early after-hours rally faded overnight as attention turned to how much it is spending on AI. Netflix was punished for a softer ad outlook.

Meta jumped more than 4% after hours, but is down by 7% on Thursday, pressured by a $9.89 billion legal charge and negative free cash flow. Netflix, which reported a day before Meta, cut its 2026 ad revenue forecast to about $2.7 billion from roughly $3 billion, and the stock closed Wednesday at its lowest level in more than two years, although it’s rebounding somewhat today.

Oppenheimer analyst Jason Helfstein covers both companies, but following their latest readouts, he only sees one as offering opportunity for investors right now.

Promotion

METQ: built for a short position on META

He starts with the bright spot at Meta. Ad revenue grew 26% excluding currency effects, and guidance points to roughly 24% growth in Q4. He credits better AI models, which let Meta charge more per ad while keeping users engaged.

He is less convinced by Muse, Meta’s new AI product. Management sounded upbeat, but the analyst notes that Muse has only about 2.5 million daily users and downloads appear to be slowing. Meta also said it needs more efficient models and more computing power before taking Muse beyond the U.S. and Canada.

Spending is the bigger worry. Annualizing Meta’s Q4 expense guidance gives a run rate of about $200 billion, which puts pressure on Helfstein’s 2027 estimate of $209 billion. He now expects 2028 EPS of $36.25, compared with the prior Street figure of about $39.29. He wants consensus to move toward $36 so it reflects costs more realistically while the payoff from AI remains uncertain. At that level, Meta trades at roughly 20x 2028 earnings, vs. 16x for Alphabet.

To this end, Helfstein reiterated a Perform (i.e., Neutral) rating for META shares without offering a fixed price target. (To watch Helfstein’s track record, click here)

For Netflix, the issue is viewing. Helfstein expects viewership to grow only in the low single digits until bigger hits arrive. That raises the question of whether revenue can keep growing at double digits without people watching more. Management says price increases, international subscribers, and ads can carry the load, and there is some support for that. U.S. and Canada revenue growth accelerated to 14% on a two-year basis, helped by ads and better retention.

Advertising is where things went wrong. Q4 revenue guidance landed about 1% below estimates because of weaker ad sales, so growth excluding currency stays at 11% instead of accelerating. Helfstein blames delays in new ad products and third-party integrations. Help is on the way, with the ad tier rolling out to 15 more countries starting in March 2027.

Q3 operating profit beat estimates by 5%, but mostly because content and marketing costs shifted into Q4. A new Chief Content Officer could improve the slate in late 2027, though the analyst expects the larger impact in 2028. He trimmed his 2026 and 2027 EPS estimates by 3% and 9%. Even so, he still expects earnings to grow around 20% a year, driven by 10% to 11% revenue growth, wider margins, and buybacks. In a downside scenario, he sees shares bottoming near $57, about 10% below where they traded when he wrote.

So where does that leave him? Helfstein keeps an Outperform (i.e., Buy) rating on NFLX stock, yet lowered his price target from $85 to $80, implying 19% upside from current levels. The target is based on 18x 2028 earnings, below Spotify’s 24x and the peer average of 20x.

Among Helfstein’s colleagues, most support META stock, making the consensus view a Strong Buy, while its $851.03 average price target offers one-year upside of 32%. NFLX claims a Moderate Buy consensus rating, its $84.79 average target suggesting shares will gain 26% in the months ahead. (See META stock forecast or NFLX stock forecast)

data.title: ‘The Right Moment,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
At the end of September, Micron (NASDAQ:MU) reported the best quarter in its history and guided to an even bigger one, yet that has done nothing for the stock. Since the start of October, the six largest memory and storage makers have lost over $1 trillion in combined market value (not accounting for today’s rout), and Micron has fallen with them. The selloff has been driven by concerns across the industry, including Chinese competition, claims that new AI models need less memory, and new factories set to come online later in the decade, as well as broader doubts over how long the AI spending boom can last.

But for top investor Louis Gerard, now is the time to get busy picking up MU shares, albeit in a cautious manner. Gerard, who ranks among the top 5% of investors on TipRanks, had been holding off on Micron until the company cleared two specific hurdles: a strong first-quarter outlook and a large share buyback. Both have now happened, so the question is whether the lower share price is a warning or an opportunity.

Regarding the first hurdle, on guidance, Gerard wanted a first-quarter outlook above $55 billion, and Micron guided to $61.5 billion at the midpoint, comfortably ahead of Wall Street’s expectations. That came after fiscal Q4 revenue of $54.23 billion, an 87% gross margin, and $33.2 billion in adjusted free cash flow.

Promotion

Curious why XOVR invested in Kalshi? Explore the long-term strategy behind the investment.

On the buyback, Micron approved a $35.16 billion program that starts in early December. The company ended the year with $68.3 billion in net cash. Gerard points out that this includes $12.7 billion in customer deposits that can generally be refunded. Excluding them leaves about $55.6 billion that truly belongs to the company.

Visibility has also improved. Micron now has 26 strategic customer agreements, up from about 16 in June, and more than three-quarters of fiscal 2027 output is already committed. Price caps in some of these deals could limit upside, but Gerard argues that giving up some upside in exchange for price floors should earn a memory company a higher multiple.

The investor goes into the industry worries in some detail. China’s CXMT plans to launch server memory built on a more advanced DRAM design by year-end, about two years before Samsung is expected to. DeepSeek claims its latest model needs a quarter of the HBM its predecessors did. SK hynix and Samsung have new capacity due in 2028 and 2029. Apple’s interest in Chinese memory suppliers adds to the risks.

On valuation, Micron trades at about 12x non-GAAP earnings, compared with roughly 31x for Nvidia and 19.6x for SanDisk. Its EV/EBITDA of 8.8x is near the bottom of its peer group, its free cash flow yield has risen to 5.8%, and its forward GAAP P/E on fiscal 2027 estimates is just over 5x.

All told, Gerard shares some of the market’s unease. But given the numbers and how much demand is already locked in, the investor sees the pullback as a chance to upgrade Micron from Hold to a cautious Buy. (To watch Gerard’s track record, click here)

Wall Street is in agreement here. The stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, based on 27 Buys and 1 Hold. Going by the $1,621.67 average price target, a year from now, shares will be changing hands for an 86% premium. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: Sandisk vs. Intel: Only One AI Stock Is a Buy Ahead of Earnings, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) both report quarterly results on October 29, and they arrive there after a remarkable year. Both stocks have soared in 2026, but both have pulled back sharply in recent weeks and are lower again today, as doubts over how the AI build-out is being funded, and whether it will pay off, continue to weigh on the chip sector.

So, does either one look like a buy going into earnings? Ahead of the anticipated prints, top investor Julia Ostian looked at both and came away with quite different views.

Starting with Sandisk, the investor sees the recent drop as more about mood than about the business. Several causes have been behind the selloff: rising bond yields, reports that Oracle’s data center projects were delayed, weak early numbers from Samsung, and news that Chinese chipmaker CXMT had made progress on its technology. Ostian points out that CXMT makes DRAM, a product Sandisk doesn’t sell at all, yet Sandisk fell as much as the DRAM makers did. The Chinese competitor that actually matters here is YMTC.

Promotion

Two ETFs to trade SNDK long or short: SNXX & SNDQ

The business itself is doing very well. Last quarter, revenue rose 372% from a year earlier, and roughly two-thirds of the growth over the prior quarter came from higher prices. Gross margin reached about 85%, up from around 26% a year earlier. EPS came in well above management’s forecast. Even so, the stock fell after that report because of the outlook. Management forecast gross margin of 83% to 85% for the current quarter, which puts the midpoint slightly below the 84.6% it had just reported.

The main thing to understand, though, is Sandisk’s long-term contracts. Eight customers have committed to at least $93.9 billion of purchases at guaranteed minimum prices. These deals will cover more than half of Sandisk’s output this fiscal year. They make earnings more predictable, but they also limit how high margins can go, since contract volume is expected to earn around 80%.

Micron’s recent results give a useful hint about Sandisk’s quarter. Micron’s NAND revenue rose 42% from the previous quarter, with prices up about 30%. Ostian doesn’t expect Sandisk to match that, because of the price limits in its contracts and slower growth in how much it can sell. What matters most on October 29 is the outlook, and the investor wants to see price growth that keeps up with the wider market.

On valuation, Sandisk trades at about 6.4 times expected earnings for the year. Its forecast for this quarter alone is more than 60% of last year’s total earnings. If earnings stayed at that level for the rest of the year, the stock would still trade below 8 times earnings. The big risk is that the supply shortage ends, for example if large cloud companies cut their spending plans.

“If you don’t own it yet, this entry is better than what we had a few weeks ago, but I’d rather split the position around October 29 than go all in before the guidance,” Ostian, who ranks among the top 5% of investors on TipRanks, said. “The ride, as promised, is not easy and will probably stay volatile.”

All told, Ostian rates SNDK stock a Buy. (To watch Ostian’s track record, click here)

Intel’s last quarter was also impressive. Revenue grew 25% from a year earlier, and earnings per share were more than double what management had forecast. That was Intel’s seventh beat in a row. Its data center and AI segment earned more profit than its PC segment, and much of the PC strength came from higher prices rather than more chips sold. The foundry business is losing less money, but it still earns very little from outside customers.

Expectations are now very high. Over the past 90 days, analysts raised their earnings estimates 30 times and lowered them zero times. That’s despite management guiding for Q3 revenue roughly flat with Q2, as tight supply means most new capacity only arrives late in the quarter. After seven straight beats, Wall Street is betting Intel will clear its own bar again, which means a modest beat may not be enough.

Capital spending is above $20 billion this year and will rise further, while free cash flow is negative. A share sale of about $23 billion also spreads profits across more shares. Ostian will be watching the Q4 outlook most closely, since a forecast below about $16.9 billion could hurt the stock even if Q3 is strong.

The valuation is the main problem. At today’s price, Intel trades at about 60 times this year’s expected earnings and about 44 times next year’s. Measured against 2028 estimates, the multiple is still around 30. Only when you look out to 2029 estimates does it fall to about 18, below the tech sector median of roughly 22. In other words, investors are paying now for profits that are three years away.

“So I, personally, don’t see this as a great buying opportunity, neither ahead of the earnings nor as a long-term position,” the 5-star investor summed up. “The only opportunity I see here is in the possible return of the sentiment, not in the fundamentals, and for me, that’s not a good enough reason to buy Intel right now.”

Accordingly, Ostian rates INTC stock a Hold.

In general, the Street feels the same way. The analyst consensus rates SNDK stock a Strong Buy, its $2,205.59 average price target suggesting shares will gain 72%. INTC is given a Hold, although its $113.28 average target offers 12-month upside of 30%. (See SNDK stock forecast or INTC stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Hold Your Horses,’ Says RBC Ahead of Oracle Stock’s Investor Day
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) is a company that has changed a lot over a short period of time. Once known as a steady, somewhat old-school database and business software company, it is now one of the most closely watched names in the AI trade. Its cloud infrastructure arm, OCI, has been signing huge deals to supply computing power for AI workloads, so the story is now as much about data centers, power and big spending budgets as it is about software.

That shift has made the stock exciting and nerve-racking at the same time. Investors like the size of the contracted pipeline, but they worry about the cost of building all that capacity and how long it will take to turn into cash. Evidently, the worriers currently make up the bigger camp, given the stock is down by 52% over the past year.

The shares could get a boost, however, from the company’s Investor Day on October 28, held during its Oracle AI World event in Las Vegas.

Promotion

High conviction ORCL bears now have this Tradr ETF

RBC analyst Rishi Jaluria will be at the event, and he will be watching several areas, starting with the infrastructure business.

OCI revenue more than doubled in fiscal Q1, up 121% year-over-year, and Oracle’s backlog of signed but not yet recognized revenue now stands at about $664 billion. What the analyst wants to hear is when margins on the AI infrastructure side will settle into the 30% to 40% range management has guided to. A recent force majeure notice tied to Project Jupiter makes that question more pressing. He is also keen to learn how much of the 10-plus gigawatts of secured capacity is actually coming online, and how the funding mix changes after 2026. That mix includes customers bringing their own hardware and paying upfront.

The applications business matters just as much to the analyst. Cloud software sales grew 10% in the quarter, with Fusion up 14% and industry-specific apps growing more than 20%. He wants to know whether AI agents are cutting implementation times and drawing more on-premises customers into the cloud, and how Oracle plans to charge for its agent-building tools. There is also the question of whether the company’s unified sales push can keep its momentum after this year’s sizeable layoffs. Signs that customers are going live faster could give the shares a boost.

Then there are the long-term goals. Oracle is aiming for $225 billion in revenue and $21 in EPS by fiscal 2030. This year’s guidance calls for roughly 34% constant-currency revenue growth and $8.10 in adjusted EPS, so the target implies earnings rising more than two and a half times in three years. Jaluria will be listening for whether management raises those targets now that capacity is arriving faster. He will also watch how operating margins hold up as lower-margin infrastructure becomes a bigger part of the mix.

Cash flow is his final concern. With Oracle in a peak spending phase, the analyst wants a clear sense of when the heavy investment gives way to stronger free cash flow, ideally backed by return-on-capital data. Next week, Oracle has to show that its AI expansion can be profitable, not just big.

“Stepping back,” Jaluria summed up, “we head into the event in wait-and-see mode as we await further visibility on OCI’s capacity ramp and margin trajectory alongside clearer performance expectations for the applications business.”

All told, Jaluria maintained a Sector Perform (i.e., Neutral) rating, although he might as well have said Buy, given his $165 price target implies shares will climb 30% higher over the one-year timeframe. (To watch Jaluria’s track record, click here)

Three other analysts join Jaluria on the sidelines, although an additional 27 Buys and 1 Sell add up to a Strong Buy consensus view. Shares are expected to gain 94% over the coming months, considering the average target clocks in at $246.11. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Can’t See the Forest for the Trees,’ Says Investor About Rocket Lab Stock
data.description:
Investors have soured on Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) stock in recent months, and October has proven to be particularly rough. Midway through the month, the space company said Neutron, its reusable medium-lift rocket, won’t fly this year after inspections found air pockets in a carbon-fiber dome on the first-stage propellant tank. Shares fell more than 10% on the news and now trade at around $52, 66% below May’s peak.

This is Neutron’s second tank problem in 2026. In January, a first-stage tank burst during a pressure test. Rocket Lab traced that failure to a defect in a section hand-laid by an outside contractor and moved production onto an automated machine. The newest flaw turned up in that new process.

So, is the share price meltdown merited or are investors facing a big opportunity right now?

Promotion

55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

An investor going by the name of Infinity Curve (IC) has been studying the setback and argues the new date matters less than the reason behind it. Two separate tank defects suggest Neutron’s real hurdle is manufacturing maturity, meaning whether Rocket Lab can reliably build its largest composite parts. There is some progress. Engineers recreated the porosity issue, fixed the manufacturing process, and built an aft dome that came out in better shape. The forward dome is now the key piece, with first-stage assembly and testing slated for Q1 2027. IC sees the second half of 2027 as the most realistic launch window and warns that another hiccup could push it into the second half of 2028.

Still, IC thinks the market now values Rocket Lab almost entirely on Neutron and overlooks the rest of the business. Q2 revenue jumped 62% year-over-year to $234 million. Space Systems, which builds spacecraft, satellite parts and solar arrays, made up 81% of sales. Backlog reached a record $2.36 billion, and about 45.5% of it should turn into revenue within a year. Electron is also adding orders. Synspective booked 20 more launches for 2028–2031, which brings its total to 47 and pushes Rocket Lab’s launch backlog past 100. IC doesn’t think Electron can carry the valuation by itself, but it acts as proof that the company can build and fly rockets.

The roughly $8 billion Iridium deal would add steady communications revenue. IC likes how it was funded: Rocket Lab sold about 29.3 million shares at an average of around $66.35, raised roughly $1.94 billion, and dropped a planned $3.6 billion bridge loan. The catch is that management will be closing its biggest acquisition while fixing its hardest engineering problem.

As for valuation, RKLB trades at about 29.4x forward EV/sales. That is far above Kratos at 3.5x forward sales, but below AST SpaceMobile at roughly 80x and SpaceX at about 42x. IC doesn’t call the stock cheap, but thinks the premium is easier to justify after the drop.

“I am more bullish on RKLB because the stock correction has created a good risk-reward setup while Rocket Lab’s fundamentals keep improving,” the investor summed up. “The Neutron’s delay increases the risk of execution, but Space Systems, Electron, and Iridium become increasingly important engines of growth.”

Bottom line, Infinity Curve rates RKLB stock a Strong Buy. (To watch Infinity Curve’s track record, click here)

data.title: SK hynix vs. Nvidia: One AI Chip Stock Is Cheap, the Other Only Looks That Way, Says Top Investor
data.description:
SK hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) are two of the biggest names behind the AI buildout, and they sit on opposite sides of the same server rack. Nvidia designs the GPUs that train and run most of today’s AI models, while SK hynix makes the high-bandwidth memory stacked alongside those chips, a market it has led for the past few years. When AI spending rises, both tend to benefit, and when sentiment turns, both tend to get sold.

That is roughly what has happened this month. SK hynix has been caught in a sharp selloff in Korean chip stocks, driven by worries over interest rates, AI spending and high memory prices, and Nvidia has slipped from its early-October high as stress at AI cloud providers like CoreWeave weighed on chip names.

So where does that leave investors right now?

Promotion

High conviction NVDA bears now have this Tradr ETF

A top investor using the nom de plume of The Techie (TT) has been taking a close look at both stocks and comes away with very different views.

On SK hynix, the investor’s starting point is demand, which TT believes has not cracked. TrendForce recently raised its spending forecast for the nine largest cloud providers, now expecting combined capex to roughly double to $957 billion in 2026 and top $1.5 trillion in 2027. ASML’s CEO added that chipmakers are already asking about equipment for 2029 and 2030. Meanwhile, SK hynix’s newest high-bandwidth memory, HBM4, is ramping with yields close to those of the previous generation.

TT, who ranks among the top 4% of investors on TipRanks, doesn’t wave away the risks. Samsung expects to win a bigger slice of the HBM market, and TrendForce sees SK hynix’s share of HBM output falling to about 50% in 2026 from 59% in 2025. China’s CXMT plans a denser server DRAM design, and equipment suppliers including ASML and Applied Materials are raising prices. The investor’s point is timing. Most of this pressure hits in 2027, not in the quarter SK hynix reports next week. Long-term deals with around 10 customers, typically running about five years and backed by deposits, should soften the blow when it arrives. What TT will be listening for on the call is any sign that 2027 HBM pricing is flat or falling.

Valuation is where TT believes the case gets hard to ignore. SK hynix trades at about 5.4x expected 2026 earnings, and its forward EV/EBITDA of 3.1x compares with a tech sector median of around 13.7x and Micron’s 3.8x. To TT, the stock already looks priced as if the 2027 debate has been lost, which is why the investor rates SKHY a Buy. (To watch The Techie’s track record, click here)

Turning to Nvidia, TT’s concern is that the company’s largest customers are becoming its competitors. Microsoft just unveiled its Maia 300 chip, which it says produces 40% more AI tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, and plans to make it the main engine for running its own AI products from 2027. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and OpenAI all have their own silicon too. Nvidia still dominates training, but TT expects most future compute growth to come from inference, and every workload a hyperscaler moves to its own chip gives it more bargaining power over Nvidia’s prices and margins.

China adds to the pressure. IDC data shows Nvidia’s share of the country’s data center AI chip market fell to 34% in the first half of the year, with Huawei close behind at 28%. Then there are the neoclouds. Gartner now predicts that more than 80% of them will lose their independence by 2030, and Nvidia has put billions into names like CoreWeave and Nebius. In TT’s view, the customers Nvidia helped fund are the ones credit markets are now treating as risky.

On paper, Nvidia looks cheap, with a forward P/E of about 23.7x and a PEG ratio under 0.5x, both lower than its peers. TT warns those numbers only work if growth estimates hold, and custom chips, China, and the neoclouds are exactly what threatens them. “While I do think the right time to buy NVDA stock will come, it is not now,” the 5-star investor summed up.

Accordingly, TT rates NVDA stock a Sell.

The Street agrees with only 50% of TT’s thesis, as both stocks claim Strong Buy consensus ratings. Over the next year, SKHY stock is expected to gain 78%, given the average target stands at $254.70. Meanwhile, NVDA’s average target lands at $323.45, a figure pointing to 12-month returns of 46%. (See SKHY stock forecast or NVDA stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Still Not Right,’ Says Investor About Rocket Lab Stock
data.description:
For a little over two years, space company Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) looked like it could do no wrong. The stock climbed more than 4,000% before peaking in May, helped along by excitement over SpaceX’s upcoming IPO. It has since almost two-thirds of its value. The most recent hit came last week, when the company pushed the first flight of its Neutron rocket into 2027 after inspections found air pockets in a carbon-composite part of the first-stage fuel tank.

An investor using the moniker The Insiders Forum (TIF) has been watching the slide closely. TIF thinks much of the drop was overdue. At its peak, the stock was priced at roughly 51 times projected 2028 sales and about 580 times projected 2028 earnings. Neutron is now more than two years late, and higher interest rates have weighed on growth stocks across the board.

The investor also has doubts about Rocket Lab’s pending purchase of Iridium Communications and its 66-satellite network, which is due to close in mid-2027. The deal turns Rocket Lab into a fully integrated space company, but the price is high. At the current share price, Rocket Lab is paying about five times Iridium’s expected 2027 sales and 33 times its earnings, and it is taking on $1.8 billion of debt. It is also issuing around 72 million new shares to buy a business that isn’t growing quickly. TIF expects arbitrage traders to keep pressure on the stock until the deal closes.

That’s not to say TIF dismisses the business. In the second quarter, backlog rose 137% to $2.36 billion, and revenue jumped 62% to a record $234.1 million. Gross margin widened to 41.5%, and about 45% of the backlog is expected to turn into revenue within a year. Since the quarter ended, Japan’s Synspective has signed up for 20 radar satellite launches between 2028 and 2031. Rocket Lab also holds an $816 million defense contract to build 18 missile-tracking satellites. The company has more than $4 billion in cash and very little debt, and most analysts rate the stock a Buy.

data.title: Tesla and Meta Earnings Are Coming: One Mag 7 Stock Is a Strong Buy, the Other Has Run Too Far, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Two of the market’s most closely watched names step into the spotlight together today, with Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) both releasing third-quarter results after the closing bell. The pairing comes at very different moments for each of these Mag 7 names. Despite today’s gain, Tesla stock is still down heavily year to date, as worries about its margins remain, while Meta has enjoyed a strong run since rolling out its Muse AI agent.  

A top investor using the pseudonym Envision Research has taken a look at both ahead of the reports and comes away with very different views on each.

Starting with Tesla, Envision’s case rests on the idea that the company is partway through switching from one way of cutting costs to another. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3, beating Wall Street’s expectations and edging past the 480,126 it delivered in Q2, though that is still about 2% below the same quarter last year. Since 2024, quarterly deliveries have bounced between roughly 300,000 and 500,000 without breaking through the top of that range.

Promotion

High conviction META bears now have this Tradr ETF

To gauge the cost side, the investor uses Wright’s Law, the idea that a product’s unit cost falls by a fixed percentage every time cumulative output doubles. Ford’s Model T tracked the curve almost perfectly, with costs falling about 15% per doubling. Tesla’s record is messier, which Envision attributes to the pace of technological change at the company. Split into two periods, before and after the gigafactories began mass production, each followed a decline of roughly 10% per doubling. The latest data point has flattened, though, with unit costs barely moving as deliveries added up.

Gross margin is also under pressure, falling to 16.9% last quarter from about 20% to 21% in the December 2025 and March 2026 quarters, hurt by smaller regulatory credit sales, lower selling prices, and rising costs. With tough competition in China and pricey fuel and raw materials, Envision expects that pressure to last for now. Analysts seem to agree, with 19 downward EPS revisions against just 5 upward ones ahead of the report. The valuation is stretched too, at more than 200x earnings.

Envision, however, sees all of this as short-term noise. When the gigafactories ramped up after 2018, they put Tesla on a new cost curve, and the investor expects the same to happen as Full Self-Driving matures and production of the Optimus robot and the Cybercab picks up. This time the savings would come from AI and robotics rather than from building more cars, which Envision considers a far more powerful source of cost cuts.

As such, Envision rates TSLA a Strong Buy. (To watch Envision Research’s track record, click here)

For Envision, Meta’s story begins with who owns it. Data from DataRoma, which tracks well-known “super-investors,” ranks Meta as the group’s fifth most widely held stock and eighth by portfolio weighting. Their average cost is around $566 per share, well below the current $733, and that gap got Envision thinking.

Much of the climb from about $550 came on the back of Meta’s AI progress, capped by the launch of the Meta Enterprise Platform, which offers businesses and developers tools such as the Muse agent, Meta Business Agent, and Muse Code. Envision likes the idea of selling Meta’s full AI stack but thinks the share price already reflects the upside. Building the platform will take more money, and spending is already heavy. Operating cash flow used to cover capex about three times over, but now does so by only about 6%, leaving free cash flow near $1.7 billion versus more than $15 billion at its recent peak. Hiring top AI talent and standing out from rivals add further uncertainty.

Fund flows point to cooling enthusiasm. Institutions own about 80% of the shares and pumped in a net $104 billion over the past year, but quarterly buying has shrunk sharply since topping $130 billion in Q4 2025. Put/call ratios are still bullish at 0.92 for volume and 0.51 for open interest, though both have crept higher during the rally.

On valuation, Meta trades at about 24x forward earnings. With EPS growth beyond 2026 expected at roughly 14% to 17%, that works out to a PEG of about 1.5x to 1.8x, above the 1x many growth-at-a-reasonable-price investors look for. The super-investors bought in at closer to 19x, and over the past three years, dips below 20x have usually been followed by multiple expansion.

“After examining these developments, I feel urged to caution investors about the downside at the current price levels,” the 5-star investor summed up. “The gap between the average holding price of professional investors and the current market price has become too wide, and the strong money seems to be repositioning their chips already.”

To this end, Envision Research rates META stock a Hold.

On the Street, TSLA stock claims a Moderate Buy consensus view, while its $402.47 average price target implies shares will gain 4.5% over the coming months. META is rated a Strong Buy, its $828.28 average target pointing to one-year returns of 18%. (See TSLA stock forecast or META stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Nothing of the Sort,’ Says Investor About Sandisk Stock
data.description:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) stock has had a bumpy ride these past few months. After an amazing run that saw the shares gain more than 5,000% over the span of a year, the stock has shed 41% since peaking in June, with October’s selling especially acute after China’s CXMT reignited competition fears by unveiling new DRAM technology and plans to enter the server memory market by year-end,

At the same time, traders appear to have locked in profits as questions around how much longer the memory boom can last have come to the fore.

The selling comes a little over a week before Sandisk reports its fiscal first-quarter results on October 29, with much of the recent chatter focused on slowing NAND prices and the growing presence of Chinese memory makers.

Promotion

SNDK has a long & short ETF? Explore SNXX & SNDQ

Top investor Kumquat Research (KR) takes those concerns seriously. Chinese investment bank GF Securities expects NAND price gains to slow to low single digits quarter-over-quarter in Q4. China’s YMTC keeps announcing technical advances, raising worries about a repeat of solar panels and EVs, where Chinese supply drove prices down.

Even so, KR argues that NAND pricing remains firm, though demand is diverging. Data center operators are still buying storage for AI buildouts, while smartphone sales are softening because higher memory costs have pushed companies like Apple to raise prices. TrendForce expects enterprise SSD prices to keep climbing in Q4 as hyperscalers place larger orders. Many of those orders are for QLC drives, a dense, lower-cost type of flash used to hold AI context data that would otherwise sit in more expensive DRAM and HBM.

In KR’s view, weaker consumer demand matters less because data centers now make up most of the market. Sandisk estimates they accounted for about 30% of NAND demand last year and roughly half today. The company also expects the NAND market to reach $300 billion this year and $500 billion in 2027.

KR uses that 2027 forecast to look at valuation. By the investor’s estimate, if Sandisk keeps its current market share and margins stay near today’s levels, it could earn about $50 billion that year. That’s roughly a quarter of its current market value, or about 4x potential 2027 earnings.

The estimate depends on supply staying tight, and Micron recently backed that view. CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said he expects conditions to be much tighter in 2027 and 2028 than in 2026, with the industry still short of supply even as NAND bit shipments grow in the mid-20% range.

KR concludes that fears about the end of the memory cycle aren’t supported by the data. With AI spending potentially topping $1 trillion in 2027 and the three biggest memory makers prioritizing DRAM and HBM over NAND, the investor expects Sandisk to keep benefiting.

“Despite the run to this point, I think SNDK is nowhere near its peak,” the 5-star investor summed up. “I am confident in memory’s prospects going into the next two years and will be holding my position throughout this near-term downtrend.”

To this end, Kumquat Research reiterated a Strong Buy on SNDK stock. (To watch Kumquat Research’s track record, click here)

data.title: ‘At This Price? You Must Be Kidding,’ Says Investor About SpaceX Stock
data.description:
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) shares are surging today, up by 9% as of writing after the company reported its first quarterly profit since going public in June. Investors also appear excited by news that SpaceX and Tesla have each set up special committees to explore a possible merger.

No doubt, the headline figures look impressive. Revenue climbed 161% year-over-year to $14.6 billion, and SpaceX booked $4.4 billion in net income, compared with a loss of about $1.1 billion in the same quarter last year.

Yet, as the stock pushes higher, taking it all in, investor Bohdan Kucheriavyi isn’t convinced the celebration is warranted. For a start, the profit looks better than the underlying business. Operating income was only about $2.8 billion, with the rest coming from items such as interest earned on IPO cash and a tax benefit.

Promotion

High conviction SPCX bulls now have this Tradr ETF

The bigger worry, though, is spending. Capital expenditures reached $19.6 billion in the quarter, almost three times the $6.9 billion of a year earlier, and the AI unit, now called Super Intelligence, accounted for $16.4 billion of that. Over the first nine months of the year, SpaceX spent $48.1 billion while generating just $13.1 billion in operating cash flow, which leaves free cash flow at roughly negative $35 billion.

Debt is piling up too. SpaceX reportedly wants to borrow around $40 billion more to buy Nvidia chips. Kucheriavyi understands the logic given strong demand for computing power, but the company already carries over $35 billion in debt and leases, and quarterly interest costs rose to $675 million. New borrowing would push total obligations past $75 billion just as rates climb and the market starts asking hard questions about how the AI boom is being funded. Plans to break into the wireless business would only add to the bill.

Shareholders also face dilution. The Cursor deal brought $23.4 billion in equity awards that will be expensed as they vest, and up to 1.3 billion shares become eligible for sale when a lockup ends Thursday. With Tesla worth over $1 trillion, any merger would almost certainly be paid for in stock.

The valuation picture has weakened as well. The share count rose to 13.58 billion from 13.18 billion, while cash fell to $89.9 billion from around $100 billion. By Kucheriavyi’s cash flow math, the shares were already trading roughly 23% above fair value before today’s jump, and full-year capex near $68 billion could push that gap wider.

There are bright spots. Connectivity operating income nearly doubled to $2.4 billion, Super Intelligence posted $5 billion in adjusted EBITDA, and Starship reached orbit last month. A strong showing from Starlink Mobile could also surprise to the upside.

Still, with profits dwarfed by cash burn and dilution looming, Kucheriavyi remains bearish on SpaceX, believing the current share price “makes no sense.” Accordingly, Kucheriavyi rates the stock a Sell. (To watch Kucheriavyi’s track record, click here)

data.title: ‘Read the Fine Print,’ Says Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) has spent the past year reinventing itself. Once known mainly for databases and enterprise software, it is now one of the most aggressive builders of AI computing capacity. It is signing huge contracts and bringing new data centers online as fast as it can.

The latest quarter showed the pivot is working, at least on the top line. Cloud infrastructure sales more than doubled year-over-year, up 121% to $7.4 billion, and total revenue rose 30% to $19.3 billion. Remaining performance obligations (RPO), meaning contracted revenue not yet booked, reached $664 billion.

Investor Lee Bailey doesn’t dismiss any of this as hype. In the investor’s view, the demand is real and already showing up in sales. The harder question is how much will be left for shareholders once Oracle has built, financed and eventually replaced all that equipment.

Promotion

ORCZ: built for a short position on ORCL

Take the backlog, for example. According to Oracle’s filings, only about 13% of it is expected to become revenue within the next 12 months. The rest is spread over years of construction and delivery. Bailey also flags customer concentration. The investor points to the reported $300 billion computing deal with OpenAI and notes that Oracle hasn’t revealed how much of its backlog depends on OpenAI, or what protections it has if the deal falls through.

Cash is another sticking point. In fiscal 2026, capital spending of $55.7 billion far exceeded operating cash flow of $32 billion, so free cash flow was deeply negative. Last quarter’s operating cash flow also included roughly $11.4 billion in customer prepayments. Bailey sees that as helpful financing but not recurring profit.

There is also around $288 billion in future data-center lease payments, mostly running 15 to 19 years. That is far longer than the six-year AI contract Oracle has used as an example. On top of that, Oracle issued about 141 million new shares during the quarter, diluting existing holders.

At first glance, the stock looks inexpensive at roughly 16 times its fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS guidance of $8.10. Bailey argues that a software-style multiple doesn’t fit a business that now depends so heavily on hardware. The investor’s model points to an expected annual return of about 7%, below the 12% a year Bailey wants to see before taking on this level of risk. Justifying today’s price would require AI infrastructure operating margins of roughly 25.6% by fiscal 2031, compared with the 17% Bailey assumes.

That leaves the investor with a Sell rating. “I want to see sustained project-level margins, healthy cash generation beyond customer advances, fewer financing surprises, and proof that older hardware can still earn attractive returns. If Oracle delivers, I’ll change my valuation,” Bailey summed up. “For now, I’m willing to miss some upside rather than pay today for cash flows that may take years to materialize.”

On the Street only one analyst joins Bailey in the bear camp, while an additional 27 Buys and 4 Holds all add up to a Strong Buy consensus rating. The forecast calls for 12-month returns of 90%, considering the average target clocks in at $249.11. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: ‘The Bottom Is Far From In,’ Says HSBC About CoreWeave Stock
data.description:
CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) stock has been taking a big beating recently. The shares are now trading roughly 55% below their 52-week high after losing about a quarter of their value last week, the stock’s worst weekly showing since November.

The trigger was debt. On October 14, shares sank 15.5% as yields on CoreWeave’s unsecured bonds climbed toward 15%, a sign lenders want a steep premium to keep funding the neocloud’s expansion. The selling continued in Tuesday’s session.

So, might now be a good time to pick up shares of the neocloud player at a discount? According to HSBC analyst Abhishek Shukla, the answer is a firm no. Already a CRWV bear, Shukla sees nothing in the selloff to change that view. The analyst argues that strained debt markets and slowing growth among LLM providers are now adding to problems built into the neocloud model from the start.

Promotion

High conviction CRWV bulls now have this Tradr ETF

The core issue is how much revenue CoreWeave earns from each megawatt of capacity. Shukla expects about $12 million per MW in 2027, compared with $17 million to $18 million for hyperscalers like Microsoft Azure, Amazon AWS, and Google Cloud. The bigger players can rent capacity on pricier short-term deals, run a general-purpose cloud business that is harder to copy, and serve many smaller clients who buy their entire tech stack. CoreWeave mostly rents bare-metal GPUs to a few very large customers, which is a far more commoditized business.

CoreWeave’s reliance on debt makes it hard to break out of that position. Neoclouds fund growth with borrowed money, and lenders want repayment locked in. That steers companies like CoreWeave toward long-term contracts with big, creditworthy clients and away from the more profitable short-term market. CoreWeave did sign some three- to six-month deals in September worth around $40 million per MW annually. But Shukla thinks softer LLM growth could weaken demand for spot capacity, and rising yields could discourage neoclouds from building capacity before customers commit.

Margins are the next concern. More than 70% of a neocloud’s costs are fixed. Depreciation alone takes about half of revenue, because GPUs are written off over six years while every $100 of gross assets brings in only around $33 a year. Data center rent and power costs aren’t falling either. Shukla models a long-term non-GAAP operating margin of 15% to 16%, well short of management’s guidance of about 25%. The analyst’s 2028 to 2030 EPS estimates sit 50% to 70% below consensus.

Against that backdrop, the valuation looks stretched. On HSBC’s estimates, CoreWeave trades at 14.7x 2030 EV/non-GAAP EBIT after stock-based compensation, versus 7x to 11x for the hyperscalers. It also trades at 0.78x EV/RPO, against Oracle’s 0.34x. Average ROIC for 2026 to 2030 comes to 8.9%, below the company’s cost of borrowing. “The more the company invests with this return profile, the more the value destruction, in our opinion,” Shukla said.

Accordingly, Shukla reiterated a Reduce (i.e., Sell) rating and an unchanged $39 price target, which implies 38% downside from current levels. (To watch Shukla’s track record, click here)

data.title: Should You Buy Netflix Stock Before Earnings Hit? This Investor Says the Market Is Missing the Point
data.description:
Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) steps up to the earnings plate today, with the streaming giant set to report third-quarter results after the closing bell, and the mood around the stock is far from upbeat. Shares have shed 44% over the past year as viewing growth cools, rivals compete for screen time, and the company works through the aftermath of its failed bid for Warner Bros. Discovery. Management has responded with a leadership reshuffle and job cuts aimed at refocusing spending on growth.

Against that backdrop, expectations going into the print are modest. In July, Netflix guided for Q3 revenue growth of 11.7% year-over-year, down from 13.4% in Q2, and narrowed its full-year sales range to $51 billion to $51.4 billion.

An investor using the moniker Summit Research (SR) doesn’t dismiss the problems. Viewing hours grew just 2% in the first half of the year, and industry data suggests audiences are dropping off in later seasons of original shows. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted last month that growth isn’t moving as quickly as he’d like. Big creative names have also walked out the door. The Duffer Brothers left for Paramount, Shawn Levy went to Disney, and David Fincher chose not to renew his deal. Meanwhile, YouTube keeps winning TV time, and Netflix’s share of U.S. TV viewing fell to a multi-year low of 7.8% in July. Rising inflation and the prospect of further rate hikes could also squeeze household budgets and advertising spend.

However, SR takes a positive stance and argues that viewing hours are the wrong yardstick. Live events take up roughly 5% of Netflix’s content budget and account for about 1% of viewing. Even so, six of the platform’s ten biggest sign-up days over the past five years came from live programming. This matters because the fourth quarter has a heavy sports lineup, including NFL games on Thanksgiving Eve and Christmas Day and the Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua fight in December. Netflix still expects its ad revenue to roughly double this year to about $3 billion. SR also points out that advertising money for live sports is moving away from traditional TV. Connected TV’s share of U.S. live sports ad spending is projected to climb from $3.5 billion this year to $7.2 billion by 2030.

SR also sees pricing power holding up. Retention stayed solid after Netflix raised U.S. prices in March. Third-party data from Apptopia showing a jump in churn tracks app inactivity rather than actual cancellations. The year-earlier quarter also had an unusually strong draw in the Taylor-Serrano boxing rematch, which makes the comparison tougher. At $8.99 a month, the ad-supported plan is also cheaper than most competing ad tiers, which could help keep cost-conscious subscribers on board.

SR’s view is that the selloff has already priced in a lot of bad news. In the investor’s opinion, the market is underestimating how much more revenue Netflix can earn from each member, and SR stays bullish heading into tonight’s report.

data.title: ‘Much Ado About Nothing,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) is one of three companies that dominate the global memory chip market, alongside SK hynix and Samsung. Its DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) products are used in the servers and AI accelerators behind the data center boom, which has made Micron one of the biggest winners of the AI era.

Since the summer, though, the shares have lagged and now sit 25% below June’s high. Investors worry that memory prices may be close to peaking, and an announcement from a Chinese competitor has made them more nervous.

However, a top investor using the pseudonym Oakoff Investments (OI) thinks those fears are overblown and remains bullish on the stock. OI argues that the risks are real but that the potential rewards still outweigh them.

Promotion

Explore why XOVR invested in Kalshi and how it identifies innovative private companies before they reach the public markets.

The biggest recent worry is CXMT, which unveiled a new vertical-transistor DRAM design and managed to send the whole memory segment into a tailspin last week. But OI notes that it is only a concept, not something ready to sell. It would also be very hard to manufacture and would need EUV lithography machines that China cannot import. Even if CXMT succeeded, China makes up only a low single-digit share of Micron’s expected FY2027 revenue. CXMT also doesn’t compete in HBM, and Micron’s management says it is about two technology generations ahead in DRAM.

OI, who ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, also points to other pressures on the stock, including rising Treasury yields and a strike vote at Micron’s Taiwan plant. OI sees these as short-term worries rather than a threat to the bigger picture.

Meanwhile, Micron’s outlook for Q1 FY2027 shows no sign of slowing down. Management expects about $61.5 billion in sales, up from $54.2 billion in fiscal Q4, and EPS of around $38, compared with $33.42 last quarter. Gross margin is expected to slip slightly to roughly 86% from 87%, but the CFO says that level should be the lowest of the year, with revenue rising every quarter.

Additionally, OI thinks supply will stay tight. HBM uses about three times as much wafer space as standard DDR5. Newer production nodes add fewer bits per wafer than before, and new factories can take two to three years before equipment can even be installed. All of this should help keep prices firm.

On valuation, analysts expect FY2027 revenue to roughly double (up about 107%) and EPS to rise around 134%. The investor thinks margin strength could push EPS growth closer to 165%, which would put the stock at only about 4.4 times forward earnings. Since growth is expected to slow to about 17% in FY2028, OI believes the market will eventually value the stock at 8 to 10 times earnings.

There are risks, of course. Memory is a cyclical business, so if prices soften and higher volumes don’t make up for it, earnings could fall. Micron’s strategic customer agreements may also limit how much it can raise prices, and competition remains a factor. OI admits that peak earnings may arrive sooner than many expect.

Even so, the investor sees agentic AI as a potential new source of memory demand that few people are counting on yet. “Nobody knows exactly how it’s going to shape the demand side in the next 3-5 years in this tech niche, but I’d bet on a positive outcome for Micron and its peers,” the 5-star investor summed up. “In the medium term, I see an upside potential of over 80%, which is why I think that the current correction is not going to last too long.”

Accordingly, Oakoff Investments rates Micron a Buy. (To watch Oakoff Investments’ track record, click here)

The Street agrees. Based on 27 Buys, 1 Hold and 1 Sell, the analyst consensus rates the stock a Strong Buy. Over the next year, shares are expected to appreciate by 74%, given the average target clocks in at $1,585.93. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: Rocket Lab Stock’s Order Book Keeps Growing, But Is That Enough? Top Investor Chimes In
data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) has spent 2026 stacking up record-setting agreements, from missile-defense satellite work for the U.S. Space Force to a hefty batch of hypersonic test launches for the Pentagon. The space company added another one at the end of September, when Japanese Earth-observation firm Synspective signed up for 20 more launches on Rocket Lab’s small Electron rocket.

It is the largest commercial contract Electron has ever won. It also brings Synspective’s total booked missions to 47, which makes the radar-satellite operator Rocket Lab’s biggest launch customer by a wide margin. The new flights are scheduled to run from 2028 through 2031.

5-star investor Rich Smith, who contributes to The Motley Fool, thinks the deal is worth a closer look, partly for what it reveals and partly for what it doesn’t. Rocket Lab kept the price private. Smith therefore works from the company’s last advertised rate of $8.4 million per Electron launch, assuming no price hike and no bulk discount. On that basis, he estimates the order is worth roughly $168 million, or about $42 million a year across the four-year window. Rocket Lab says the contract lifts its launch backlog above 100 missions. By the same math, Smith puts that backlog at more than $840 million in future revenue.

Still, the investor sees Neutron as the real swing factor. Neutron is Rocket Lab’s reusable medium-lift rocket. It can carry about 13 tons to low Earth orbit, roughly 40 times what Electron can lift. Yet its reported price is only about six times that of an Electron launch. Smith says that combination gives Rocket Lab two advantages. It can go after customers with much larger satellites and earn more per mission. And a lower cost per kilogram could let it undercut SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and win business from it.

The catch is timing. Last week, Rocket Lab pushed Neutron’s first flight into 2027 and did not set a firm date. Even after Neutron starts flying, the company plans to launch it just once in its first year, three times in its second, and five times in its third. Smith notes that few analysts surveyed by S&P Global Market Intelligence expect Neutron to make Rocket Lab profitable right away, so Electron will still be doing most of the work for years.

As Rocket Lab is still losing money, the stock can’t yet be valued on profits. Smith believes the pending Iridium acquisition is what changes that. The roughly $8 billion deal is expected to close in mid-2027. Smith expects it to make Rocket Lab profitable and free-cash-flow positive that year, whether or not Neutron is flying by then. “Once that happens, it will become a whole lot easier to value Rocket Lab based on its profits and decide whether it’s a stock worth buying,” Smith, who ranks among the top 5% of investors on TipRanks, summed up.
